content.description: In the 5th century BC, Athens invented a system where citizens governed directly. Selection by lot, an equal right to speak, and exclusion on a massive scale.

hero.hook: How one Greek city invented the power of the people, and ran into its limits.

blocks.text: In the 5th century BC, Athens invented something radical: **[[Politics]]**, in the sense that citizens were no longer the subjects of a king but the authors of their own fate. Power (*kratos*) belonged to the people (*demos*). That is where the word democracy comes from.
This direct democracy, born out of crisis and reform, is still a reference point for Western political thought, with its strengths and its blind spots.

In the 7th century BC, Athens was torn between aristocrats and farmers crushed by debt. **[[Solon]]**, a statesman elected in **594 BC**, abolished debt slavery and opened public office to wealth rather than birth alone.

The real turning point was **[[Cleisthenes]]** (**508-507**). This reformer created **10 mixed tribes** to break up the clans, and set up the **[[Boule]]**, the Council of Five Hundred chosen by lot. Every citizen could now serve the city.

blocks.caption: The Agora of Athens, the heart of civic life

blocks.text: To push out a man who had grown too powerful, Athenians voted for **[[Ostracism]]** by scratching his name on a shard of pottery: ten years of exile, with a quorum of **6,000** voters.

sections.title: Reforms that opened up the city

blocks.text: In the middle of the 5th century, under **Pericles**, a general reelected fifteen times and the face of the Athenian golden age, the system opened wider. The **Ecclesia**, the assembly of citizens, met about **40 times** a year on the hill of the Pnyx. It voted on laws, on war, on peace and on the budget.

blocks.caption: Pericles, reelected general fifteen times and the face of the Athenian golden age

blocks.text: **[[Isegoria]]** guaranteed an equal right to speak. The **[[Misthos]]**, a daily allowance, let the poorest citizens take their seats. Justice ran through the **[[Heliaia]]**: **6,000** jurors drawn by lot. Choosing by lot kept anyone from capturing power, except among the military generals.

Out of roughly **300,000** inhabitants, only **30,000 to 50,000** male citizens voted. Women, slaves and metics (resident foreigners) were shut out. In **451**, Pericles tightened the rule further: a citizen now needed two citizen parents.
A founding paradox: equality among peers rested on slavery and exclusion. A face-to-face democracy, intense but closed.
A man who took no interest in public life was called an *idiotes*, a “private person.” The word gave us “idiot”: cutting yourself off from the common good looked like a failure of reason.

sections.title: A democracy that excluded most people

blocks.text: A [[Demagogue]], a speaker who flatters the passions of the crowd, could carry the assembly on emotion alone. **Plato**, a philosopher marked by the death of his teacher **Socrates** (**399 BC**), saw in democracy the rule of opinion over truth, and the textbook case of the tyranny of the majority.

For all its flaws, Athens left ideas that lasted: leaders answerable for their acts, equality before the law, argument in the open. Selection by lot and direct democracy are even coming back into today's debates.

events.detail: The dark side of popular sovereignty.
events.title: Death of Socrates

blocks.text: Athenian democracy was direct rule by free male citizens, built on selection by lot and an equal right to speak. It left out about **85%** of the population, but it invented Western public debate.

content.title: Who really held power in Athenian democracy?

Boule.explanation: Council composed of 500 citizens drawn by lot (50 per tribe) responsible for studying draft laws before their presentation to the Ecclesia.

Cleisthenes.explanation: Athenian reformer (508-507 BC) considered the true founder of democracy. He reorganized the city into 10 mixed geographical tribes, breaking traditional family solidarities in favor of political citizenship.

Demagogue.explanation: An orator seeking to win the people's favor by flattering their passions rather than by appealing to their reason.

Heliaia.explanation: The supreme popular court of Athens, whose members were chosen by lot from among volunteer citizens.

Isegoria.explanation: The equal right for every citizen to speak before the assembly of the people (Ecclesia).

Misthos.explanation: Financial allowance paid to Athenian citizens to compensate for the loss of income linked to the exercise of public duties (courts, assembly).

Ostracism.explanation: Athenian procedure by which citizens could vote to exile for 10 years a man judged dangerous for democracy. Names were inscribed on pottery shards (ostrakon). Its objective was preventive, not punitive.

Politics.explanation: From the Greek 'polis' (the city). Refers to the art of managing the city's affairs and the space for common deliberation between citizens.

Solon.explanation: Athenian statesman elected archon in 594 BC to resolve a social crisis. He canceled debts, abolished debt slavery, and reorganized the city by wealth rather than birth - the first step toward democracy.
